content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued detailed recommendations and guidance on HIV testing services, emphasizing evidence-based practices and person-centered care. 1. Demand Creation for HIV Testing Services: Strategies to increase the uptake of HIV testing services (HTS) are essential for reaching individuals at high risk of HIV who are unaware of their status. These strategies also help reduce stigma, discrimination, and criminalization. Effective demand creation approaches include peer-led interventions, digital platforms (e.g., short videos promoting testing), and targeted messaging during counseling sessions. Messages focusing on risk reduction, economic empowerment, and motivational content have shown positive results. Less effective methods for demand creation include personal invitation letters, general text messages (e.g., SMS), and counseling focused solely on building client-counselor relationships. Incentives can increase testing uptake but must be carefully evaluated for sustainability, equity, and long-term behavioral impact. 2. Facility-Based HIV Testing: In high HIV burden settings, routine HIV testing should be offered to all clients (adults, adolescents, and children) in clinical settings. In low HIV burden settings, testing should be offered to clients presenting with symptoms or conditions indicative of HIV, such as tuberculosis (TB) or sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Routine testing should also be considered in settings like antenatal care (ANC), malnutrition clinics, and services for key populations. 3. Community-Based HIV Testing: Community-based HIV testing services are recommended, especially for key populations, to complement facility-based testing. These services should include linkage to prevention, care, and treatment. 4. Self-Testing for HIV and Other Infections: HIV self-testing (HIVST) is recommended as an additional option for HIV testing services. It does not replace provider-administered testing but can complement it, especially for underserved populations. Self-testing for syphilis (SST) and hepatitis C virus (HCVST) is also suggested as part of broader testing programs. Clear instructions and support tools (e.g., videos, peer support) should be provided to ensure proper use and interpretation of results. Dual HIV/syphilis self-tests and other quality-assured products should be used where available. 5. Retesting Recommendations: Key populations should be tested at least annually, with more frequent testing (e.g., biannually or quarterly) based on risk. Pregnant women in high HIV burden settings or from key populations should be retested in the third trimester or during labor and delivery. If missed, catch-up testing is necessary. Individuals reporting recent HIV exposure should be tested and offered post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) or pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) as appropriate. Retesting within 14 days is advised for inconclusive results or suspected acute infections. 6. HIV Testing Algorithms and Strategies: HIV testing algorithms should achieve at least 99% positive predictive value (PPV) and use tests with high sensitivity (≥99%) and specificity (≥98%). Countries are advised to use three consecutive reactive tests to confirm an HIV-positive diagnosis. Western blotting and non-line immunoassays should not be used in national testing strategies. HIV recency testing is not recommended as part of routine HIV testing services but may be used for surveillance purposes. 7. Post-Test Services and Linkage to Care: Rapid antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation should be offered to all individuals with a confirmed HIV diagnosis following clinical assessment. Support interventions, such as enhanced linkage with case management, patient tracing, and peer support, should be provided to ensure timely engagement in care. ART initiation should follow person-centered care principles, respecting individual dignity and preferences, particularly for vulnerable populations. 8. Partner Services for STIs and HIV: Partner services for individuals with STIs or HIV should be voluntary and never coercive. Privacy and confidentiality must be upheld. A range of partner service options, including patient referral, provider-assisted referral, and expedited partner therapy (EPT), should be offered based on patient preferences and available resources. 9. Lay Provider HIV Testing: Trained and supervised lay providers can safely and effectively conduct HIV testing using rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs). 10. Integration and Quality Assurance: All testing approaches, including self-testing, should be integrated into broader health programs and ensure linkage to further testing, care, and treatment. Quality-assured products and services are essential for all testing strategies. These recommendations aim to optimize HIV testing services, improve access, and ensure timely linkage to care while addressing the diverse needs of populations at risk.
